title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Lake Township limits data center water and power draws as more towns push back.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're diving into Lake Township's new push to cap how much water and electricity data centers can use.
That's right in Huron County, right? A rural spot where folks are worried about their wells and the local grid.
Exactly. The township is drafting stricter zoning rules after residents raised alarms about big facilities straining resources.
This feels like part of a bigger wave. We've seen similar moves popping up across the state lately.
It is. Lake Township is writing limits on water and power draws for any new data centers, and the draft comes as more AI companies scout Michigan sites.
Why now? What's the history here that has residents so concerned?
Rural areas like this have seen proposals for large server farms that need massive cooling systems, which pull a lot of water. Power demand can spike too, hitting the local grid hard.
And that directly affects everyday folks, like higher electric bills or wells running low during dry spells.
Right. In places with farmland and small towns, one big facility can change the water table or force upgrades that ratepayers end up paying for.
Who are the main players pushing back? Is it mostly residents or local officials too?
Residents have been vocal about protecting their wells and keeping the grid stable. Officials are responding with these zoning tweaks to give the township more control upfront.
What happens next? Do these rules go to a vote soon, or is this still early drafting?
It's a draft right now, but the township is moving to finalize them as companies keep eyeing the area for AI servers.
And if they pass, how might that change the game for future projects statewide?
It sets a precedent. Other townships are watching and doing the same, tightening standards on size, noise, and utility use before anything gets built.
We've got stories from Lyon Township and the Detroit suburbs today showing the same pattern.
Exactly. Hundreds showed up in Lyon Township to oppose noise and truck traffic from a proposed site near homes.
They testified it could hurt property values and daily life within a mile. The township hasn't voted yet.
And around Detroit, suburbs are rewriting zoning to give boards more say over power spikes and location.
That could mean higher bills for southeast Michigan ratepayers if big projects connect without checks.
Negaunee City just approved its own ordinance setting clear standards on size, noise, and power before projects even reach planning.
That prevents rushed deals that strain city services and the grid.
Over in Marshall, police confirmed credible threats against council members amid the data center debate over power, noise, and tax breaks.
They're considering extra security while the review continues in Calhoun County.
University of Michigan picked a Textile Road site in Washtenaw County for its own data center, which will add power demand and affect local rates and services.
And in Saline Township, an attorney is challenging a tax abatement for Oracle's big campus that would skip years of property taxes.
Taxpayers there would cover the lost revenue while the project pulls heavy power and water.
Yesterday we also saw DTE and Consumers pushing regulators on rate hikes tied to data center demand.
Lawmakers are being asked to scrap automatic annual increases and rethink how utilities earn money as billions in new power costs come online.
A court fight over one of DTE's AI data center contracts is also raising questions about the utility's growth plans.
If that unravels, it could delay serving massive new loads in southeast Michigan, with ratepayers feeling the backup costs.
And Iosco County is drafting rules to limit size, noise, and power in the East Tawas area as big tech looks north for cheap land.
It's the same story playing out in different spots: locals wanting guardrails before projects land.
Back to Lake Township though. How do these caps actually work in practice?
The rules would set hard limits on water withdrawals and electricity draws, forcing companies to scale or find other sites if they exceed them.
That protects the rural character and existing users like farms and homes.
Data centers need constant cooling, so water use can be huge in summer. Power is steady and massive, sometimes equivalent to a small city's demand.
And in a place like Huron County, one facility could tip the balance on both.
Residents worry about wells going dry and blackouts or higher bills from grid strain.
What about the companies? Are they pushing back on these new rules?
Not specifically in Lake Township yet, but the pattern statewide shows firms looking for places with fewer restrictions.
So stricter zoning could steer them elsewhere or force better designs.
Right. Some projects get redesigned with more efficient cooling or on-site generation to meet local limits.
And that could mean slower rollout but maybe fewer conflicts down the road.
The stakes go beyond one township. These rules ripple to electric rates across the region.
Because utilities spread costs, a reader 30 or 60 miles away feels it in their monthly bill.
Farmland conversion is another angle. Once land goes to data centers, it's hard to go back.
And small towns lose control if they don't act early on zoning.
Lake Township is trying to get ahead of that.
How many other places have done something similar recently?
Quite a few. Negaunee just locked in rules, Iosco is drafting, and suburbs near Detroit are rewriting theirs.
It shows a coordinated local response to the AI boom.
What happens next in Lake Township specifically?
The draft moves forward, public input continues, and a final vote could come in the next few weeks.
If approved, it becomes a model other rural townships might copy.
And companies will have clearer expectations before investing.
On the power side, it ties into those bigger rate debates we saw yesterday with DTE and Consumers.
Exactly. Local caps can influence how much new demand hits the statewide grid.
Listeners in other counties should watch how this plays out.
Now let's hit the other stories quickly.
Lyon Township residents packed a meeting against noise and traffic from a proposed data center.
They say it would affect property values and life within a mile, and the township hasn't voted yet.
Detroit suburbs are also tightening zoning after complaints about noise, water, and grid strain.
That gives local boards more say and could protect ratepayers from surprise costs.
Negaunee approved an ordinance with clear standards on size, noise, and power.
It stops rushed proposals that could overload services.
In Marshall, credible threats against council members emerged over a data center fight on power and incentives.
Police are involved and extra security is on the table.
U-M chose Textile Road for its data center, impacting Washtenaw County power and taxes.
Saline Township faces a challenge to its Oracle tax abatement that would shift lost revenue to taxpayers.
Yesterday DTE and Consumers asked to lock in bigger profits tied to data center demand.
Regulators want to overhaul rate hikes so costs don't automatically pass to residents.
A legal challenge to one DTE AI contract could delay its growth plans.
Iosco is drafting rules to curb sprawl in the East Tawas area.
Now for on deck.
Monday the Kalamazoo City Commission will vote on a temporary moratorium on data center development.
That's a chance for residents to weigh in on pausing new projects while rules get sorted.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Lake Township Draws the Line on Data Center Water and Power
